simple: Dijkstra that also looks at how far each place still is from the goal.
analogy: Ravi's "ridden so far plus crow-flies distance".
precise: best-first search ordered by f(n) = g(n) + h(n), where h estimates the remaining cost; with an admissible heuristic it returns an optimal path, and with a consistent heuristic it never needs to reopen a node.
source: D2 of F9-54 (Peter E. Hart, Nils J. Nilsson, Bertram Raphael, "A formal basis for the heuristic determination of minimum cost paths" (1968)) — pending verification (dossier gate G1 open)

simple: a guess of the remaining distance that is never too big.
analogy: the crow-flies distance is never longer than the ride.
precise: h(n) ≤ h*(n) for every node, where h* is the true remaining cost.
source: D2 of F9-54 (Peter E. Hart, Nils J. Nilsson, Bertram Raphael, "A formal basis for the heuristic determination of minimum cost paths" (1968)) — pending verification (dossier gate G1 open)

simple: the list of pairs of things that are allowed to touch.
analogy: fingers are allowed to touch the box they are grasping.
precise: a table of (body, body) pairs whose contacts are ignored by collision checking, such as adjacent links, or the gripper and the object during a grasp.
source: D1 of F9-57 (MoveIt 2 documentation) — pending verification (dossier gate G1 open)

simple: given more and more time, the route gets as short as possible.
analogy: Mira's route home improving each day.
precise: the cost of the best solution found converges (almost surely) to the optimal cost as the number of samples tends to infinity; RRT* has it, plain RRT does not.
source: D4 of F9-55 (Sertac Karaman, Emilio Frazzoli, "Sampling-based algorithms for optimal motion planning" (2011)) — pending verification (dossier gate G1 open)

simple: an object the planner treats as part of the robot because the robot is holding it.
analogy: the box in Lina's hand that must also clear the lamp.
precise: a collision object fixed to a robot link; it moves with the link, is checked against the world, and may be allowed to touch the gripper links.
source: D1 of F9-57 (MoveIt 2 documentation) — pending verification (dossier gate G1 open)

simple: a tree of small behaviours, checked from the top many times a second, that decides what the robot does now.
analogy: a cyclist's habits checked in priority order every moment.
precise: a rooted tree whose leaves are conditions and actions and whose inner nodes are control nodes (sequence, fallback, parallel) and decorators; the root is ticked periodically and every node returns SUCCESS, FAILURE or RUNNING.
source: D1 of F9-58 (Michele Colledanchise, Petter Ögren, "Behavior Trees in Robotics and AI: An Introduction" (CRC Press, 2018)) — pending verification (dossier gate G1 open)

simple: a move in which the hand follows a straight line.
analogy: lowering your hand straight down onto the box.
precise: a sequence of tool poses along a straight line (or other curve) in the workspace, converted to joints by IK at small steps; it fails if any step has no IK solution or a joint jump.
source: D1 of F9-57 (MoveIt 2 documentation) — pending verification (dossier gate G1 open)

simple: not letting a square get darker or lighter than a limit.
analogy: Lina never presses so hard that she cannot rub it out again.
precise: bounding each cell's log-odds to an interval [l_min, l_max] so that the map stays able to change when the world changes (a door opens).
source: D1 of F9-52 (Sebastian Thrun, Wolfram Burgard, Dieter Fox, "Probabilistic Robotics") — pending verification (dossier gate G1 open)

simple: testing points along a move to see whether any of them hits something; the resolution is the spacing of those points.
analogy: looking for bushes every few metres along a path.
precise: a segment is declared free if each of its sampled points is free; it can miss any obstacle thinner than the spacing. Exact (continuous) checks exist for simple shapes.
source: D1 of F9-55 (Kevin M. Lynch, Frank C. Park, "Modern Robotics: Mechanics, Planning, and Control" (Cambridge University Press, 2017)) — pending verification (dossier gate G1 open)

simple: the set of all positions the robot could be in, with the ones that would make it touch something removed.
analogy: on the map, shading the pavement too, because a bicycle is wider than a line.
precise: the space of all configurations of the robot; C_free is the subset where the robot does not intersect obstacles. For a disc robot of radius r translating in the plane, C_free is the plane minus the obstacles grown by r.
source: D1 of F9-54 (Kevin M. Lynch, Frank C. Park, "Modern Robotics: Mechanics, Planning, and Control" (Cambridge University Press, 2017)) — pending verification (dossier gate G1 open)

simple: a guess that never drops by more than the cost of a step.
analogy: riding one block never brings you closer to Grandma, as the crow flies, by more than one block.
precise: h(n) ≤ c(n, n′) + h(n′) for every edge, and h(goal) = 0; consistency implies admissibility, and f never decreases along a path.
source: D2 of F9-54 (Peter E. Hart, Nils J. Nilsson, Bertram Raphael, "A formal basis for the heuristic determination of minimum cost paths" (1968)) — pending verification (dossier gate G1 open)

simple: a grid that says, for each square, how bad it is to put the robot's centre there.
analogy: the map with dangerous streets shaded darker.
precise: a 2D grid of costs from free to lethal, built by combining layers (static map, obstacles seen by sensors, inflation) and used by planners and controllers.
source: D6 of F9-56 (David V. Lu, Dave Hershberger, William D. Smart, "Layered costmaps for context-sensitive navigation" (2014)) — pending verification (dossier gate G1 open)

simple: one source of costs on the costmap.
analogy: one transparent sheet on top of the map: road works on one sheet, parked vans on another.
precise: a plugin that writes costs into the costmap: the static layer copies the map, the obstacle layer marks and clears cells from sensor data, the inflation layer adds costs around lethal cells.
source: D6 of F9-56 (David V. Lu, Dave Hershberger, William D. Smart, "Layered costmaps for context-sensitive navigation" (2014)) — pending verification (dossier gate G1 open)

simple: deciding which thing you see now is which thing you saw before.
analogy: is this the sofa from the living room, or the bed from the bedroom?
precise: the correspondence problem between current observations and map elements or past poses; wrong associations (false loop closures) corrupt the estimate.
source: D1 of F9-53 (Sebastian Thrun, Wolfram Burgard, Dieter Fox, "Probabilistic Robotics") — pending verification (dossier gate G1 open)

simple: working out where you are only by adding up your own movements.
analogy: counting steps and turns in the dark.
precise: integrating odometry (wheel encoders, inertial data) from a known start; the error grows without bound because every step's error is added and none is ever removed.
source: D1 of F9-53 (Sebastian Thrun, Wolfram Burgard, Dieter Fox, "Probabilistic Robotics") — pending verification (dossier gate G1 open)

simple: a node with one child that changes how the child is run.
analogy: "try up to three times".
precise: a node with a single child that modifies its ticks or its status, such as retry, repeat, timeout or inverter.
source: D1 of F9-58 (Michele Colledanchise, Petter Ögren, "Behavior Trees in Robotics and AI: An Introduction" (CRC Press, 2018)) — pending verification (dossier gate G1 open)

simple: exploring outwards from the start, always continuing from the nearest place not yet finished.
analogy: Ravi's sister's plan: every street, a little further each time.
precise: a best-first search ordered by g(n), the cost of the best known path from the start to n; with non-negative costs it finds optimal paths to every node it finishes.
source: D3 of F9-54 (Edsger W. Dijkstra, "A note on two problems in connexion with graphs" (1959)) — pending verification (dossier gate G1 open)

simple: try these in order; stop at the first one that works.
analogy: the short road, or else the long way round.
precise: ticks children left to right; returns SUCCESS or RUNNING as soon as a child does, and FAILURE if all fail.
source: D1 of F9-58 (Michele Colledanchise, Petter Ögren, "Behavior Trees in Robotics and AI: An Introduction" (CRC Press, 2018)) — pending verification (dossier gate G1 open)

simple: a robot is always in one of a few named situations, and rules say when it moves to another.
analogy: a trip has stages (setting off, riding, parking), and you move between them for clear reasons.
precise: a finite set of states, one of which is current, and transitions between states triggered by events or conditions, with actions on entry, during the state or on transitions.
source: D2 of F9-58 (David Harel, "Statecharts: a visual formalism for complex systems" (1987)) — pending verification (dossier gate G1 open)

simple: how big the robot is, and how far from walls it should prefer to stay.
analogy: the width of the bike, and the extra space you like to keep from parked cars.
precise: the footprint (a radius or polygon) defines lethal cells for the robot's centre; inflation adds a cost that decays with distance up to the inflation radius, so planners prefer paths with clearance.
source: D1 of F9-56 (Nav2 documentation) — pending verification (dossier gate G1 open)

simple: from the joint angles, work out where the hand is.
analogy: knowing your shoulder, elbow and wrist angles, you know where your fingertips are.
precise: the map from joint configuration q to the pose of a link frame, built by composing each joint's transform (F9-25); for a planar chain, x = Σ L_i cos(q_1 + … + q_i), z likewise with sin.
source: D2 of F9-57 (Kevin M. Lynch, Frank C. Park, "Modern Robotics: Mechanics, Planning, and Control" (Cambridge University Press, 2017)) — pending verification (dossier gate G1 open)

simple: the part that turns sensor data into "I moved this much" and "I have been here before", and the part that combines all of those into the best overall guess.
analogy: Lina's eyes and step counting, and Lina redrawing the whole page.
precise: in graph-based SLAM, the front end produces constraints (odometry, scan-matching and loop-closure edges) from raw data; the back end solves the resulting non-linear least-squares problem over all poses.
source: D3 of F9-53 (Giorgio Grisetti, Rainer Kümmerle, Cyrill Stachniss, Wolfram Burgard, "A tutorial on graph-based SLAM" (2010)) — pending verification (dossier gate G1 open)

simple: the part that chooses the whole route, and the part that steers along it moment by moment.
analogy: reading the map at home, and steering on the road.
precise: the global planner computes a path from the current pose to the goal on the costmap (slowly, about once a second here); the controller computes velocity commands many times a second to follow the path while respecting limits and nearby obstacles.
source: D2 of F9-56 (Steve Macenski, Francisco Martín, Ruffin White, Jonatan Ginés Clavero, "The Marathon 2: a navigation system" (2020)) — pending verification (dossier gate G1 open)

simple: telling a running action to stop because something else is now more important.
analogy: braking and turning back when the phone rings.
precise: a call from a parent to a RUNNING child that is no longer selected; the action must cancel its work (for example, cancel a navigation goal) and return to idle.
source: D1 of F9-58 (Michele Colledanchise, Petter Ögren, "Behavior Trees in Robotics and AI: An Introduction" (CRC Press, 2018)) — pending verification (dossier gate G1 open)

simple: making obstacles fatter on the map so you can plan for the robot's centre as a point.
analogy: shading a bike's width along every wall.
precise: marking every cell within distance r of an occupied cell as blocked (and optionally adding a cost that decreases with distance beyond r, F9-56).
source: D1 of F9-54 (Kevin M. Lynch, Frank C. Park, "Modern Robotics: Mechanics, Planning, and Control" (Cambridge University Press, 2017)) — pending verification (dossier gate G1 open)

simple: from where the hand must be, work out the joint angles.
analogy: deciding how to bend your arm to touch a spot.
precise: solving FK(q) = target for q; it may have no solution (out of reach), several (elbow up or down), or infinitely many (redundant arms); solvers are analytic for simple arms and numerical in general.
source: D2 of F9-57 (Kevin M. Lynch, Frank C. Park, "Modern Robotics: Mechanics, Planning, and Control" (Cambridge University Press, 2017)) — pending verification (dossier gate G1 open)

simple: the rule that says what one sensor reading tells you about each square.
analogy: "darker where the light lands, lighter where it passes".
precise: p(m_i | z_t, x_t), the probability that cell i is occupied given only the current measurement and pose; called inverse because it reasons from effect (the reading) to cause (the world).
source: D1 of F9-52 (Sebastian Thrun, Wolfram Burgard, Dieter Fox, "Probabilistic Robotics") — pending verification (dossier gate G1 open)

simple: working out where the robot is on a map that already exists.
analogy: recognising the street you are on.
precise: estimating the pose in the map frame from odometry and scans, for example with a particle filter (Monte Carlo localisation), and publishing the correction as the map-to-odometry transform.
source: D5 of F9-56 (Sebastian Thrun, Wolfram Burgard, Dieter Fox, "Probabilistic Robotics" (MIT Press, 2005)) — pending verification (dossier gate G1 open)

simple: a way to store a probability as a number that you can add to.
analogy: how many pencil strokes a square has received, darker minus lighter.
source: D1 of F9-52 (Sebastian Thrun, Wolfram Burgard, Dieter Fox, "Probabilistic Robotics") — pending verification (dossier gate G1 open)

simple: noticing that you are back at a place you have already been.
analogy: recognising the front door at the end of the walk.
precise: a constraint between two poses that are far apart in time but close in space, obtained by place recognition and verified by matching; it lets the back end remove accumulated drift along the whole loop.
source: D2 of F9-53 (Hugh Durrant-Whyte, Tim Bailey, "Simultaneous localization and mapping: part I" (2006)) — pending verification (dossier gate G1 open)

simple: drawing a map when someone tells you exactly where you are each time you look.
analogy: the uncle calling out Lina's tile.
precise: estimating the map m from measurements z_1:t and poses x_1:t that are treated as given; SLAM (F9-53) removes that assumption.
source: D1 of F9-52 (Sebastian Thrun, Wolfram Burgard, Dieter Fox, "Probabilistic Robotics") — pending verification (dossier gate G1 open)

simple: a beam that did not hit anything the sensor could see.
analogy: the torch light fades out before reaching any wall.
precise: a range value reported at (or beyond) the sensor's maximum because no echo was detected; it is evidence of free space up to the range limit, never evidence of an obstacle.
source: D1 of F9-52 (Sebastian Thrun, Wolfram Burgard, Dieter Fox, "Probabilistic Robotics") — pending verification (dossier gate G1 open)

simple: the set of programs that take a robot from "go there" to arriving.
analogy: Ravi's map-reading at home plus his steering on the road.
precise: a pipeline of localisation, map representation (costmaps), global planning, local control, goal and progress checking, and recovery, coordinated by a task executive.
source: D2 of F9-56 (Steve Macenski, Francisco Martín, Ruffin White, Jonatan Ginés Clavero, "The Marathon 2: a navigation system" (2020)) — pending verification (dossier gate G1 open)

simple: a map made of small squares, each holding how likely it is that something solid is there.
analogy: Lina's squared paper, shaded darker where the torch landed.
precise: a regular tessellation of the environment into cells, each with a binary random variable "occupied"; the map stores the posterior probability of occupancy of every cell given all measurements and poses, under the assumption that cells are independent.
source: D1 of F9-52 (Sebastian Thrun, Wolfram Burgard, Dieter Fox, "Probabilistic Robotics") — pending verification (dossier gate G1 open)

simple: the places you know how to reach but have not finished, and the places you have finished.
analogy: corners pencilled on the map, and corners crossed out.
precise: a priority queue of frontier nodes ordered by f (or g), and the set of nodes already expanded; a node is expanded when it is removed from the open list.
source: D2 of F9-54 (Peter E. Hart, Nils J. Nilsson, Bertram Raphael, "A formal basis for the heuristic determination of minimum cost paths" (1968)) — pending verification (dossier gate G1 open)

simple: straightening a wiggly path by joining far-apart points when the straight line is clear.
analogy: Mira cutting corners on the way home.
precise: repeatedly pick two points of the path at random and replace the part between them by the straight segment, when that segment passes the collision check.
source: D1 of F9-55 (Kevin M. Lynch, Frank C. Park, "Modern Robotics: Mechanics, Planning, and Control" (Cambridge University Press, 2017)) — pending verification (dossier gate G1 open)

simple: the planner's picture of the world: the robot, the furniture, and the things it holds.
analogy: what Lina remembers about the kitchen while her eyes are on the box.
precise: the robot's state and collision geometry, the world's collision objects, objects attached to robot links, and the rules about which pairs may touch; every plan is checked against it.
source: D1 of F9-57 (MoveIt 2 documentation) — pending verification (dossier gate G1 open)

simple: a list of places the robot has been, with notes saying how far apart pairs of them are.
analogy: the footprints on Lina's page, joined by "four steps" notes.
precise: a graph whose nodes are robot poses and whose edges are relative-pose measurements with information (inverse covariance) matrices; SLAM finds the node poses that minimise the sum of squared, information-weighted edge errors.
source: D3 of F9-53 (Giorgio Grisetti, Rainer Kümmerle, Cyrill Stachniss, Wolfram Burgard, "A tutorial on graph-based SLAM" (2010)) — pending verification (dossier gate G1 open)

simple: a pose just above or in front of the object, from which the hand can move straight in.
analogy: Lina's hand hovering above the box.
precise: a tool pose at a fixed offset from the grasp pose along the approach direction; the free-space planner goes there, a Cartesian move does the last part.
source: D2 of F9-57 (Kevin M. Lynch, Frank C. Park, "Modern Robotics: Mechanics, Planning, and Control" (Cambridge University Press, 2017)) — pending verification (dossier gate G1 open)

simple: if a way exists, the chance of finding it grows to certainty as you keep trying.
analogy: Mira will eventually find the stand if there is any way.
precise: the probability that the planner returns a solution, when one exists (with some clearance), tends to 1 as the number of samples tends to infinity; it says nothing about how long that takes, and it cannot prove that no path exists.
source: D2 of F9-55 (Steven M. LaValle, "Rapidly-exploring random trees: a new tool for path planning" (technical report, 1998)) — pending verification (dossier gate G1 open)

simple: scatter many random free positions, join neighbours, and reuse that network for many trips.
analogy: marking good spots and safe links in the park once, then using them every day.
precise: a multi-query planner: a learning phase samples free configurations and connects each to nearby ones with free segments; a query connects start and goal to the roadmap and runs graph search.
source: D5 of F9-55 (Lydia E. Kavraki, Petr Švestka, Jean-Claude Latombe, Mark H. Overmars, "Probabilistic roadmaps for path planning in high-dimensional configuration spaces" (1996)) — pending verification (dossier gate G1 open)

simple: noticing that the robot is stuck, and trying something to get unstuck.
analogy: going round the same block twice, then walking back and asking.
precise: a progress checker fails the controller when the robot has not moved a minimum distance within a timeout; recovery behaviours (clear costmaps, back up, spin, wait) are then tried, a bounded number of times, before the goal is aborted.
source: D2 of F9-56 (Steve Macenski, Francisco Martín, Ruffin White, Jonatan Ginés Clavero, "The Marathon 2: a navigation system" (2020)) — pending verification (dossier gate G1 open)

simple: steer towards a point a little way ahead on the path.
analogy: looking a few metres ahead on the road, not at your front wheel.
precise: a path-tracking controller that picks the path point at a look-ahead distance L and commands the arc through it, curvature κ = 2y / L², where y is the point's sideways offset in the robot frame.
source: D3 of F9-56 (R. Craig Coulter, "Implementation of the pure pursuit path tracking algorithm" (technical report, 1992)) — pending verification (dossier gate G1 open)

simple: listing every square that a straight beam passes through.
analogy: the squares the torch light crosses on the paper.
precise: enumerating the cells intersected by a line segment between two cells; this chapter uses Bresenham's integer line algorithm, which visits one cell per step of the major axis.
source: D5 of F9-52 (J. E. Bresenham, "Algorithm for computer control of a digital plotter" (1965)) — pending verification (dossier gate G1 open)

simple: a reactive node re-checks everything from the start at every tick; a memory node carries on from where it was.
analogy: checking the traffic light again at every moment, or remembering that you already passed it.
precise: a reactive sequence restarts from its first child on every tick and halts a running child when an earlier one fails; a sequence with memory resumes at the running child and does not re-tick finished children.
source: D1 of F9-58 (Michele Colledanchise, Petter Ögren, "Behavior Trees in Robotics and AI: An Introduction" (CRC Press, 2018)) — pending verification (dossier gate G1 open)

simple: a tree that grows from the start towards random points.
analogy: Mira's branching trail.
precise: repeat: sample q_rand; find the nearest tree node q_near; move from q_near towards q_rand by at most a step to q_new; if the segment is free, add q_new with parent q_near.
source: D2 of F9-55 (Steven M. LaValle, "Rapidly-exploring random trees: a new tool for path planning" (technical report, 1998)) — pending verification (dossier gate G1 open)

simple: RRT that keeps improving its route.
analogy: Mira, each time she reaches a new spot, checking whether nearby spots could be reached more quickly through it.
precise: RRT plus two steps per new node: choose the parent among nearby nodes that minimises cost-from-start, then rewire nearby nodes through the new node when that lowers their cost; asymptotically optimal under conditions on the neighbourhood size.
source: D4 of F9-55 (Sertac Karaman, Emilio Frazzoli, "Sampling-based algorithms for optimal motion planning" (2011)) — pending verification (dossier gate G1 open)

simple: a planner that tries random positions and connects the good ones.
analogy: Mira's random tall trees.
precise: a planner that builds a graph or tree in C-space from randomly sampled configurations, using only a collision checker (is q free? is the segment q₁q₂ free?) and never an explicit model of C_obs.
source: D1 of F9-55 (Kevin M. Lynch, Frank C. Park, "Modern Robotics: Mechanics, Planning, and Control" (Cambridge University Press, 2017)) — pending verification (dossier gate G1 open)

simple: sliding and turning a new laser scan until it fits what you have already seen.
analogy: lining up the sofa you see with the sofa on your page.
precise: estimating the relative pose between a scan and a reference (another scan or a map) by optimising an alignment score; correlative matching evaluates the score on a grid of candidate poses.
source: D4 of F9-53 (Edwin Olson, "Real-time correlative scan matching" (2009)) — pending verification (dossier gate G1 open)

simple: a list of places and the moves between them, each move with a cost.
analogy: street corners and the streets joining them on Ravi's map.
precise: a graph G = (V, E) with non-negative edge costs; on an occupancy grid, V is the set of free cells and E joins each cell to its 4 or 8 neighbours with cost equal to the step length (times any extra cost of the cell).
source: D1 of F9-54 (Kevin M. Lynch, Frank C. Park, "Modern Robotics: Mechanics, Planning, and Control" (Cambridge University Press, 2017)) — pending verification (dossier gate G1 open)

simple: do these in order; stop at the first one that is not done.
analogy: unlock, mount, ride.
precise: ticks children left to right; returns FAILURE or RUNNING as soon as a child does, and SUCCESS if all succeed.
source: D1 of F9-58 (Michele Colledanchise, Petter Ögren, "Behavior Trees in Robotics and AI: An Introduction" (CRC Press, 2018)) — pending verification (dossier gate G1 open)

simple: building a map of an unknown place while working out where you are in it, using that same map.
analogy: drawing the map of a dark house while walking through it with a torch.
precise: estimating the joint posterior over the robot's poses (the last one in online SLAM, all of them in full SLAM) and the map, given controls or odometry and measurements, starting from an unknown map.
source: D1 of F9-53 (Sebastian Thrun, Wolfram Burgard, Dieter Fox, "Probabilistic Robotics") — pending verification (dossier gate G1 open)

simple: one "check and act" pass through the tree.
analogy: one glance at the road.
precise: a call that propagates from the root to the children chosen by each control node, and returns a status upwards; ticks are issued at a fixed rate (here every 0.5 s).
source: D1 of F9-58 (Michele Colledanchise, Petter Ögren, "Behavior Trees in Robotics and AI: An Introduction" (CRC Press, 2018)) — pending verification (dossier gate G1 open)

simple: deciding how fast to move along a planned path.
analogy: speeding up gently and slowing down before the shelf.
precise: assigning times to the waypoints of a path so that every joint's velocity and acceleration stay within limits; the path's shape is unchanged.
source: D3 of F9-57 (Tobias Kunz, Mike Stilman, "Time-optimal trajectory generation for path following with bounded acceleration and velocity" (2012)) — pending verification (dossier gate G1 open)

simple: the time written on a measurement saying when it was taken.
analogy: the time Lina wrote next to each torch look.
precise: the acquisition time carried in a message header; any algorithm that combines two sensors looks up the other sensor's state at this time, so a stamp that is late or early by Δt makes the fusion use the wrong pose.
source: D6 of F9-53 (ROS 2 documentation) — pending verification (dossier gate G1 open)

simple: A* that trusts its guess more than it should, to finish faster.
analogy: Ravi doubling the crow-flies number to hurry.
precise: best-first search on f = g + w·h with w > 1; with an admissible h, the path cost is at most w times the optimum.
source: D4 of F9-54 (Ira Pohl, "Heuristic search viewed as path finding in a graph" (1970)) — pending verification (dossier gate G1 open)
